cases.question: Which company turned FY2024-to-FY2025 revenue growth into the strongest operating income growth? Show the numbers and explain where operating leverage weakened. Distinguish improvement from a loss base from meaningful percentage growth.
cases.review: Answer the operating-leverage comparison with matching figures and cited explanations; do not treat Intel loss-base improvement as ordinary percentage growth.
cases.answer:
- NVIDIA won on meaningful operating-income percentage growth: FY2025 revenue grew 114.20% [C13], while operating income grew 147.04% [C14], from $32.972 billion [F10] to $81.453 billion [F12]. Operating margin rose from 54.12% [C15] to 62.42% [C16]. Higher Data Center mix lifted gross margin; operating expenses grew 45%, substantially slower than revenue. [S39] [S37]

- AMD ranked second: revenue grew 34.34% [C1]; operating income grew 94.42% [C2], from $1.900 billion [F2] to $3.694 billion [F4]. Margin increased from 7.37% [C3] to 10.66% [C4]. This was genuine growth from a positive, but smaller, profit base. Leverage faced headwinds from $440 million of net MI308 export-control inventory charges, R&D growth of 25%, and marketing/general/administrative expense growth of 52%. [S45]

- Qualcomm had comparatively weaker—not negative—annual leverage: revenue grew 13.66% [C18]; operating income grew 22.68% [C19], from $10.071 billion [F14] to $12.355 billion [F16]. Margin increased from 25.85% [C20] to 27.90% [C21]. Gross margin nevertheless fell from 56% to 55% because higher-margin QTL licensing contributed a smaller revenue proportion. [S60]

- Intel was loss recovery, not meaningful operating-income percentage growth: revenue declined 0.47% [C6], while operating losses narrowed from $11.678 billion [F6] to $2.214 billion [F8], a $9.464 billion improvement [C9]. Exclude it from the percentage-growth ranking. Foundry still lost $10.3 billion; reduced impairment/depreciation charges helped, while early Intel 18A ramp inventory reserves remained a headwind. [S68] [S67]

- No company’s annual operating margin deteriorated: NVIDIA expanded 8.30 percentage points [C17], AMD 3.30 [C5], Qualcomm 2.05 [C22], and Intel 17.80 from a negative base. [C12] “Weakened” therefore describes specific cost/mix pressures, not annual consolidated margin contraction.

- These are company fiscal years, not common-calendar periods. Qualcomm’s comparison uses 53 weeks in FY2024 versus 52 in FY2025, without normalization. [F13]

cases.answer:
- Intel’s FY2025 supports an early turnaround thesis, not a completed recovery: stronger server demand and lower costs coexist with declining consolidated revenue, weaker client profitability, and substantial foundry losses. [S25] [S22] [S20] [S13] [S8]

- Stronger customer demand: DCAI revenue increased $794 million versus FY2024; higher hyperscale demand helped lift server volume 9%. Second-half server pricing also benefited from higher demand. Against this, full-year server ASPs fell 4%, reflecting competitive pricing and product mix. [S25]

- Cost reductions: DCAI operating income increased $2.0 billion, primarily supported by $1.5 billion of lower operating expenses from workforce reductions and other savings. Foundry operating expenses fell $1.2 billion. These support an efficiency turnaround, but DCAI’s higher revenue benefit was substantially offset by higher server unit costs—not clear evidence of demand-driven profit expansion. [S22] [S8]

- Accounting and nonrecurring effects: Consolidated gross profit increased $1.0 billion, primarily because impairment and accelerated-depreciation charges declined. cases.answer:
- NVIDIA’s FY2025 revenue grew 114% to $130.5 billion. The disclosures establish customer concentration, not how much of that growth came from particular customers. [S12] [S9]

- Direct-customer concentration: For the year ended January 26, 2025, Customers A, B and C represented 12%, 11% and 11% of total revenue, respectively, primarily in Compute & Networking. In FY2024, B represented 13%; A and C each represented less than 10%. These are shares of annual revenue, not contributions to incremental growth. [S9]

- Ultimate-customer exposure differs: Direct customers include distributors, ODMs, OEMs and system integrators. Indirect customers include cloud service providers, consumer internet companies, enterprises and public-sector entities. A direct-customer percentage therefore does not identify a single ultimate buyer. [S8]

- NVIDIA estimated that one indirect customer represented at least 10% of FY2025 total revenue, attributable to Compute & Networking. That customer primarily purchased through system integrators and distributors, including Direct Customer B. The estimate uses purchase-order information, product specifications, internal sales data and other sources; actual revenue may differ. [S6]

- Do not add the indirect-customer threshold to the direct-customer percentages: the disclosed purchasing route overlaps with B. Nor can the anonymous direct customers be identified as hyperscalers, treated as three separate ultimate buyers, or used to establish an exact aggregate hyperscaler revenue share. [S6] [S8] [S9]

- Missing: Customer-level year-over-year revenue contributions and a complete mapping from direct channels to ultimate buyers. Without those, the portion of FY2025 growth dependent on a small customer group—and exact hyperscaler dependence—cannot be quantified from these disclosures. [S6] [S9]

arguments.question: Is Qualcomm meaningfully diversifying away from handsets? Compare FY2024 and FY2025 automotive and IoT revenue against handset revenue and consolidated revenue. Explain whether growth in smaller businesses changes the concentration picture.
arguments.answer:
- Qualcomm is diversifying, but handset concentration remains high. Automotive and IoT grew faster than handsets and gained consolidated revenue share; handset share eased from 63.81% [C8] to 62.76% [C9]—a modest change rather than a transformation.

- FY2024 → FY2025 comparison, USD:
  - Automotive: $2.910bn [F3] → $3.957bn [F7]; growth 35.98% [C5]. Consolidated revenue share: 7.47% [C3] → 8.94% [C4].
  - IoT: $5.423bn [F5] → $6.617bn [F9]; growth 22.02% [C15]. Consolidated revenue share: 13.92% [C13] → 14.94% [C14].
  - Handsets: $24.863bn [F4] → $27.793bn [F8]; growth 11.78% [C10]. Consolidated revenue share: 63.81% [C8] → 62.76% [C9].
  - Consolidated revenue: $38.962bn [F1] → $44.284bn [F2]; growth 13.66% [C16].

- Interpretation: smaller businesses are changing the mix in the right direction, especially automotive. However, handset revenue also expanded and remains substantially larger than either business. This is meaningful diversification progress, not evidence that handset dependence has ended. These handset figures represent the QCT handset revenue stream, not a comprehensive measure of all handset-linked revenue.

- Comparability: original-report annual figures; FY2024 ran September 25, 2023–September 29, 2024 and contained 53 weeks. FY2025 ran September 30, 2024–September 28, 2025 and contained 52 weeks. Growth is not week-normalized. [F1] [F2]

arguments.analysis_answer:
- Qualcomm is diversifying, but handset concentration remains high. Automotive and IoT grew faster than handsets and gained consolidated revenue share; handset share eased from 63.81% [C8] to 62.76% [C9]—a modest change rather than a transformation.

- FY2024 → FY2025 comparison, USD:
  - Automotive: $2.910bn [F3] → $3.957bn [F7]; growth 35.98% [C5]. Consolidated revenue share: 7.47% [C3] → 8.94% [C4].
  - IoT: $5.423bn [F5] → $6.617bn [F9]; growth 22.02% [C15]. Consolidated revenue share: 13.92% [C13] → 14.94% [C14].
  - Handsets: $24.863bn [F4] → $27.793bn [F8]; growth 11.78% [C10]. Consolidated revenue share: 63.81% [C8] → 62.76% [C9].
  - Consolidated revenue: $38.962bn [F1] → $44.284bn [F2]; growth 13.66% [C16].

- Interpretation: smaller businesses are changing the mix in the right direction, especially automotive. However, handset revenue also expanded and remains substantially larger than either business. This is meaningful diversification progress, not evidence that handset dependence has ended. These handset figures represent the QCT handset revenue stream, not a comprehensive measure of all handset-linked revenue.

- Comparability: original-report annual figures; FY2024 ran September 25, 2023–September 29, 2024 and contained 53 weeks. FY2025 ran September 30, 2024–September 28, 2025 and contained 52 weeks. Growth is not week-normalized. [F1] [F2]

cases.question: If I held all four companies, which demand, customer, manufacturing, and geographic risks would still overlap? Identify two apparent diversifiers that are less independent than they look. Separate filing evidence from your portfolio interpretation.
cases.review: Sourced cross-company exposures and explicit interpretation; no unsupported correlation estimate or pretense of measured portfolio risk.
cases.answer:
- Filing evidence below uses each company’s FY2025 original 10-K; fiscal periods are company labels, not a synchronized calendar-year snapshot.

- Demand overlap: All four disclose sensitivity to demand conditions, though through different markets. NVDA flags adverse economic conditions and demand/supply mismatches; AMD describes semiconductor downturns, deferred purchases and inventory adjustments; INTC flags weaker consumer spending and business IT investment; QCOM describes cyclical downturns and trade barriers reducing device demand. [S20] [S39] [S48] [S51]

- Customer overlap: Each depends on significant customers or intermediaries. NVDA customers can delay purchases or develop competing solutions, and indirect purchasing can obscure concentration. AMD expects a small customer group to remain a substantial revenue source. INTC discloses limited-customer concentration and distributor credit risks. QCOM warns that significant-customer cancellations, delays and internal chip development can reduce revenue. These establish a shared risk type—not identical customers across all four. [S34] [S37] [S40] [S55]

- Manufacturing overlap: All four retain external-supplier exposure. NVDA lacks guaranteed wafer/component capacity; AMD relies on TSMC for microprocessor/GPU wafers at 7 nm or smaller; some advanced INTC products depend exclusively on TSMC or critical TSMC components; QCOM relies on limited third-party suppliers, with foundries primarily in Asia. [S17] [S24] [S26] [S30]

- Geographic overlap: China-related policy risk reaches all four, but differently: NVDA and AMD face export restrictions; INTC reports trade restrictions affecting sales and ordering; QCOM has substantial Chinese-customer exposure and Taiwan supply vulnerability. [S18] [S21] [S47] [S49] [S45] [S32]

- Portfolio interpretation—apparent diversifier 1: INTC’s manufacturing footprint is not an independent hedge against fabless-company supply shocks. Its TSMC dependence leaves a common external-foundry channel. [S26] [S24] [S30]

- Portfolio interpretation—apparent diversifier 2: QCOM’s handset exposure provides different end-demand exposure, but not independence from customer insourcing or China policy. Those mechanisms also appear at NVDA; AMD and INTC share China-policy exposure. Different products therefore do not eliminate these common vulnerabilities. [S52] [S46] [S34] [S18] [S21] [S47]

cases.question: All four companies grew revenue in FY2025, so AI clearly lifted every business. What evidence best confirms that common growth driver? Challenge my premise if it is wrong.
cases.review: Reject Intel consolidated-growth premise and universal AI causation; distinguish company segments and qualified subset overlap.
cases.answer:
- The premise is wrong: Intel’s FY2025 revenue declined 0.47%, while NVIDIA grew 114.20%, AMD 34.34%, and Qualcomm 13.66%. [C2] [C3] [C1] [C4]

- NVIDIA provides the strongest direct AI attribution. Its FY2025 10-K explicitly says revenue growth was driven by data-center compute and networking platforms for accelerated computing and AI. Data Center computing revenue grew 162%, primarily from Hopper demand for large language models, recommendation engines, and generative AI; networking grew 51%, driven by Ethernet for AI. [S38] [S37]

- AMD supports AI as a shared driver with NVIDIA—not an explanation for every business. FY2025 Data Center revenue grew 32%, driven by EPYC processors and Instinct GPU accelerators; AMD separately reported strong demand for data-center AI GPUs. Client and Gaming growth also reflected Ryzen processors, game-console chips, and Radeon gaming GPUs, while Embedded revenue declined. [S68] [S69] [S71]

- Intel does not confirm universal AI-led growth. FY2025 DCAI revenue increased 5%, attributed to hyperscale server and networking demand—not specifically quantified AI contributions. CCG revenue declined 3%, with customer inventory reductions and manufacturing supply constraints among the disclosed pressures. Consolidated revenue fell. [S63] [S64]

- Qualcomm’s FY2025 explanation points to premium-tier Snapdragon demand, higher handset pricing and favorable mix, increased IoT shipments, and new vehicle launches using digital-cockpit products. That evidence does not isolate AI as the cause of its growth. [S60]

- Conclusion: AI-related data-center demand is supported as a common driver for NVIDIA and AMD, not all four companies. Establishing an all-four AI contribution would require attribution separating AI from other demand at Intel and Qualcomm; the retrieved disclosures do not provide that. [S38] [S68] [S69] [S63] [S60]

- These are company fiscal years, not matching calendar periods; Qualcomm’s comparison also spans 52 weeks versus 53 weeks. [F2] [F4] [F6] [F7] [F8]

cases.question: QCOM 24 vs 25: sales up, EPS down. What broke? Separate tax/accounting noise from the operating story and tell me what to ask management next.
cases.review: Interpret PM shorthand, retrieve GAAP EPS and tax explanation, distinguish operating strength from noncash charge, and preserve fiscal labels.
cases.answer:
- The main break was tax accounting, not operating earnings. QCOM FY2025 revenue rose 14% to $44.3 billion from $39.0 billion in FY2024. Pretax income increased to $12.663 billion from $10.336 billion, but net income fell to $5.5 billion from $10.1 billion. [S13] [S20]

- Tax/accounting noise: FY2025 included a $5.7 billion charge establishing a valuation allowance against federal deferred tax assets after OBBB tax reform. Qualcomm expects to remain subject to corporate alternative minimum tax beginning FY2026, preventing realization of substantially all those existing assets. This was a deferred-tax accounting hit, not an equivalent current cash-tax payment. [S13] [S14] [S18]

- But do not dismiss the entire tax story as noise. Qualcomm expects ongoing CAMT exposure. Separately, restored immediate deductibility of domestic R&D beginning FY2026 should lower cash-tax payments. The accounting charge and future cash-tax economics need separate explanations. [S14] [S18]

- Operations improved:
  - QCT revenue increased to $38.367 billion from $33.196 billion; EBT margin improved to 30% from 29%. [S15]
  - Handset growth leaned heavily on pricing/mix: $2.5 billion from higher revenue per chipset versus $423 million from higher shipments. IoT benefited from shipments; automotive benefited from new digital-cockpit vehicle launches. [S25] [S23]
  - Watch costs: QCT gross margin stayed approximately flat as higher product costs offset pricing benefits; higher operating expenses restrained EBT-margin improvement. QTL revenue and its 72% EBT margin were essentially unchanged. [S23]

- Ask management next:
  - “Bridge FY2026 cash taxes, GAAP tax expense and normalized tax expense. What persists under CAMT, and what could reverse the valuation allowance?” [S14] [S18]
  - “How durable is handset pricing/mix growth, and what happens to margins if premium demand slows?” [S25] [S23]
  - “Why did higher pricing not expand gross margin, and which product costs and operating expenses can improve?” [S23]
  - “What converts automotive/IoT shipment growth into sustained profit growth, and what returns QTL to growth?” [S23]
